data.title: Mesoblast Wins Deloitte Tech Fast 50 Leadership & Enterprise Growth Award
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mesoblast Limited (Nasdaq:MESO; ASX:MSB), global leader in allogeneic cellular medicines for inflammatory diseases, today announced it has received the Leadership & Enterprise Growth Award at the Deloitte Technology Fast 50 Australia Awards which recognizes Australia’s fastest-growing technology companies and the founders, innovators and leaders shaping the future of the sector.

The award recognizes Mesoblast’s successful evolution to a commercial-stage biotechnology company following its U.S. launch of Ryoncil® (remestemcel-L-rknd), the first mesenchymal stromal cell therapy approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).1

“We are pleased to receive this award from Deloitte which recognizes Mesoblast's leadership excellence across innovation and scalability in the healthcare industry,” said Mesoblast Chief Executive Dr. Silviu Itescu. “The successful launch of RYONCIL has established a strong commercial foundation for Mesoblast and has enabled patients to access a life changing product. We are focused on building on that foundation, progressing our broader portfolio and delivering sustainable growth and long-term value for our shareholders.”

About Mesoblast

Mesoblast (the Company) is a world leader in developing allogeneic (off-the-shelf) cellular medicines for the treatment of severe and life-threatening inflammatory conditions. The therapies from the Company’s proprietary mesenchymal lineage cell therapy technology platform respond to severe inflammation by releasing anti-inflammatory factors that counter and modulate multiple effector arms of the immune system, resulting in significant reduction of the damaging inflammatory process.

Mesoblast’s Ryoncil® (remestemcel-L-rknd) for the treatment of steroid-refractory acute graft versus host disease (SR-aGvHD) in pediatric patients 2 months and older is the first FDA-approved mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapy. Please see the full Prescribing Information at www.ryoncil.com.

Mesoblast is committed to developing additional cell therapies for distinct indications based on its remestemcel-L and rexlemestrocel-L allogeneic stromal cell technology platforms. Ryoncil® is being developed for additional inflammatory diseases including SR-aGvHD in adults and biologic-resistant inflammatory bowel disease. Rexlemestrocel-L is being developed for heart failure and chronic low back pain. The Company has established commercial partnerships in Japan, Europe and China.

About Mesoblast intellectual property: Mesoblast has a strong and extensive global intellectual property portfolio, with over 1,000 granted patents or patent applications covering mesenchymal stromal cell compositions of matter, methods of manufacturing and indications. These granted patents and patent applications provide commercial protection extending through to at least 2044 in all major markets.

About Mesoblast manufacturing: The Company’s proprietary manufacturing processes yield industrial-scale, cryopreserved, off-the-shelf, cellular medicines. These cell therapies, with defined pharmaceutical release criteria, are planned to be readily available to patients worldwide.

Mesoblast has locations in Australia, the United States and Singapore and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange (MSB) and on the Nasdaq (MESO). For more information, please see www.mesoblast.com, LinkedIn: Mesoblast Limited and X: @Mesoblast

data.title: After Anthropic's 'bittersweet' IPO, here's what lies ahead
data.description:
By William Gavin

Retail investors showed up, but Anthropic has so far failed to provide a broad lift to the technology sector

Anthropic just debuted on the Nasdaq.

The true test of Anthropic's initial public offering lies in the weeks and months ahead - when more investors will have the ability to both buy and sell shares in a referendum on the state of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic ended up selling more shares than expected in its IPO - and at a higher price - as its stock debuted Thursday on the Nasdaq. In terms of proceeds, Anthropic (ANT) had the biggest IPO to date, breaking SpaceX's (SPCX) record and leaving the company with ample coffers to help fund the AI boom.

However, the stock's early momentum faded on Thursday, ending the day up just 17% from its IPO price. Shares had opened 34% higher before giving back some gains.

Anthropic had a non-diluted market capitalization of $1.28 trillion at the close.

Some people may "call it lackluster next to other tech IPOs, but it's debatable whether a bigger pop is desirable, since that could suggest Anthropic left more money on the table," said James Kisner, an analyst at Water Tower Research, via email.

Kisner added that the IPO's execution was "bittersweet," since it poured cold water on the idea that Anthropic could lift the broader market.

Anthropic went public in less-than-ideal conditions, with fear over everything from high inflation to Nvidia's (NVDA) CEO succession struggles and concerns over export policies weighing down on stocks. Kieran Osborne, chief investment officer at Mission Wealth, noted some investors may have trimmed their other tech stakes to buy Anthropic shares.

According to Dow Jones Market Data, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, S&P 500 SPX, Nasdaq Composite COMP and Russell 2000 RUT are each on pace for their worst week since April 4, 2025.

While Anthropic may not be the tide that raises all boats, the IPO still represents an "important milestone" for the AI sector, said Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson. After all is said and done, Anthropic will also have more than $230 billion in cash, based on the details of its IPO and its latest financial statements.

"Anthropic now has an enormous war chest it can use to buy more compute from its providers, primarily Amazon, Google and SpaceX. Those companies in turn now have visibility to buy more chips from Broadcom, Nvidia and Micron," Luria told MarketWatch over email. Compute refers to chips and other hardware.

Nick Smith, an analyst at Renaissance Capital, said Anthropic's "pretty strong debut" also is a good signal for future IPOs. He noted that several companies may be ready to launch after Thanksgiving, including Nscale (NSCL), which has a $44.6 billion deal to provide AI computing power to Anthropic. OpenAI, Anthropic's chief rival, is also considering an IPO as soon as 2027.

"However, we will see where Anthropic's trading goes from here and what impact that might have," Smith added.

Retail investors made Thursday the biggest day ever for retail participation in an IPO going back to at least 2012, according to Vanda Research. Demand for shares from Robinhood Markets (HOOD) was "far greater" than it was allocated, its chief executive said.

Meanwhile, institutional investors tend to play the long game and wait for a better price to emerge before buying into a newly public stock, said Baird Managing Director Ted Mortonson. Their decisions in the coming weeks will have a big impact.

Anthropic will also soon start to get added to major stock indices - likely including the Nasdaq-100 NDX. Insider-owned shares subject to early lockups will also begin to expire. Hundreds of millions of shares were released for trading on Thursday, and another 174 million class A shares will be released next month.

"We won't know the depth of demand until we see those shares come unlocked," said Ben Black, chief investment officer at Powerlaw.

-William Gavin

This content was created by MarketWatch, which is operated by Dow Jones & Co. MarketWatch is published independently from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: US Market Crash: Dow Jones tanks 1,100 points, nears technical correction - What is plaguing Wall Street?
data.description:
Benchmark indices on Wall Street ended sharply lower on Thursday, November 19, as the mega and historic listing of Anthropic PBC failed to sustain the enthusiasm around the AI trade as multiple issues continue to bother market participants. The initial bout of gains was quickly sold into and the selling only accelerated through the session.

The Dow Jones tanked 1,100 points on Thursday, taking the four-day fall for the index to 3,250 points. The index had entered a "Technical Correction", meaning a 10% fall from the peak at its intraday low. The index also closed below the mark of 50,000 for the first time since June this year.

The day was no different for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, as despite the Anthropic listing, other names sold-off and dragged both the indices lower by over 2% each. 460 stocks on the S&P 500 ended with losses on Thursday, indicating the extent of the adverse market breadth.

Wall Street's volatility gauge, the CBOE VIX crossed the mark of 29 intraday and is now at the highest level since March this year.

Anthropic Makes A Historic Debut

Anthropic PBC became the first AI lab to go public, debuting at a hefty premium to its already upsized issue price.

The stock began trading at $111.5 per share, a 34.3% premium to its revised IPO price of $83 apiece. At listing, Anthropic's market capitalization had crossed the mark of $2 trillion.

At the close of the session, Anthropic shares saw some profit booking from the highs to close at $97.7, still a 17% premium from the issue price, valued at $1.8 trillion, making it the seventh most valuable US company.

AMD In The Line Of Fire

After Nvidia, which has now been issued subpoenas by the Attorney General's office in California, its rival Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell prey to a short-seller report on Thursday.

The stock fell 8% on Thursday after short-seller Hunterbrook Media, after disclosing short positions on the stock, said that AMD kept supplying new devices to IEIT Systems, a Chinese server manufacturer, despite the company being blacklisted by the US.

Hunterbrook's note also stated that AMD bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong, and also depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips.

In response, AMD stated that it remains fully compliant with US export controls and that Hunterbrook has misrepresented its business practices and relationships.

What Are The Issues Plaguing Wall Street?

Anthropic's IPO was supposed to reinstate some faith in the AI trade, but concerns continued to overshadow not just the tech names, but also the entire Wall Street.

Soon after the Anthropic IPO, democrats lashed out at Anthropic, with some calling it a "ticking time bomb" and a "trojan horse" for hackers and foreign adversaries.

The mega capex planned by these companies also remains an area of concern. After massive debt fund raising, SpaceX is now eyeing a debt sale of $32 billion. That, coupled with the credit market stress, fears of higher interest rates for longer, and geopolitical concerns continue to plague Wall Street.

Sell-off also continued in Gold and Silver, with the Yellow Metal now set for its worst losing streak since May, and Silver prices declining over 65% from their peak of over $120 an ounce.

data.title: Amazon Urges NYC Customers to Oppose Mamdani-Backed Delivery Bill — WSJ
data.description:
By Isabella Simonetti

The war between New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Amazon.com is heating up.

On Thursday, when New Yorkers opened Amazon's app or visited its website, a warning appeared: "NYC Council Could add up to $5 per order."

The notice refers to the Delivery Protection Act, a City Council bill backed by Mamdani that calls for warehouse operators such as Amazon to obtain licenses from the city by adhering to new safety, training and employment requirements.

It also would require Amazon to directly hire couriers who are currently employed by smaller firms that deliver its packages.

"As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we're doing this," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill. "

The warning on Amazon's website links to a form where customers can input their names and addresses. It then automatically drafts a message to their council member.

"As your constituent, I am writing to urge you to oppose Intro 518, a bill that threatens to raise costs for New Yorkers like me," it reads. "This bill could increase my annual delivery costs by up to $664 per year. In a city already facing an affordability crisis, that's money I cannot afford to lose — and neither can my neighbors."

Amazon launched this campaign roughly a week before Black Friday, one of the biggest shopping days of the year, and said that within the first six hours of its debut, New York City customers sent approximately 20,000 emails to council members urging them to oppose the legislation.

Mamdani fired back on X.

"Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company," he wrote. "If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed," he continued, referring to the Amazon founder.

Aside from supporting the Delivery Protection Act, which was introduced by New York City Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, Mamdani has taken other actions that target Amazon. Earlier this year, he announced the collection of more than $9 million in idling fines from Amazon delivery vehicles. Mamdani also sent cease-and-desist orders to online retailers, including Amazon, that the city said were selling illegal e-bikes.

Amazon has previously said it requires e-bikes sold in its store to meet applicable safety standards. The company also said it has worked with city officials to resolve idling fines, adding that many of them didn't reach Amazon's Delivery Service Partners, independent companies that deliver packages, because of gaps in how violations were tracked.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin also chimed in on Amazon's campaign early on Thursday.

"It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers' cost of living if it's forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections," she wrote on X. "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs. If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong."

Write to Isabella Simonetti at isabella.simonetti@wsj.com

data.title: Japan's Tama Home paid up to 18% repair commissions
data.description:
Japanese housebuilder Tama Home , already facing a scandal over fraudulent fire insurance claims made by its employees, paid sales staff commissions of as much as 18% on the home repair contracts they won, Yomiuri Shimbun reported on November 20.

Non-life insurers are pressing for a third-party committee to investigate the company, and they have raised concerns about the pay scheme. The newspaper said the scheme is likely to become a focus of that inquiry, and that some employees may have filed false claims again and again to raise their earnings. By November 19, the country's three largest non-life insurers had stopped selling new policies through Tama Home.

An internal investigation report obtained by Yomiuri Shimbun showed that the company paid sales staff incentive pay on certain jobs, including maintenance, repairs and renovation work. The rate ran from roughly 2% to 18% of the profit on each job, calculated as revenue minus costs. Staff received 2% when the profit was below JPY100,000 ($626) and 18% when it reached JPY5mn or more.

When fire insurance covers a repair, the insurer's payout goes towards the cost of the work. The newspaper said fraudulent payouts would therefore have inflated Tama Home's sales and profits. That in turn would have raised the commissions of the employees handling those jobs.

The company also ran a separate programme for its highest earners by annual sales. Winners received cash awards of up to JPY100,000 and trips abroad.

The false claims began no later than around 2020. In some cases, staff reused photographs from earlier accidents to support unrelated claims. The internal investigation confirmed roughly 340 fraudulent cases at the Takamatsu branch, worth a combined JPY23mn.

In June, Tama Home carried out a nationwide internal review. Staff reported about 120 further cases outside Takamatsu in which fictitious claims were suspected. The company did not classify these as fraud, saying it had no objective evidence. The insurers' own checks have found suspected cases at other locations, and the insurers want a third-party committee to conduct a full investigation.

data.title: Citi incorrectly booked trades, underestimated risky assets by $35 billion, sources say
data.description:
By Tatiana Bautzer and Elisa Martinuzzi

Citigroup incorrectly booked trades at a European subsidiary that underestimated its risk-weighted assets, two people familiar with the matter said, in a setback for the US lender that has been trying to fix regulatory issues.

Citigroup underestimated risk-weighted assets by about $35 billion at a trading unit in Europe, one person familiar with the matter said.

In a statement to Reuters, Citigroup said the bank had identified and resolved an internal capital modeling issue at a European trading subsidiary this summer. "The subsidiary remained fully compliant with regulatory minimums throughout, with no impact on the holding company or main operating bank," the bank said. "Citi completed remedial actions and injected capital to immediately restore the subsidiary's buffers."

The mishap is a setback for Citi CEO Jane Fraser, who has been trying to get the bank out of the regulatory penalty box for years. Citi has operated under tight supervisory scrutiny and as recently as the summer, was targeting submitting paperwork to regulators this year to get the restrictions lifted, Reuters has reported.

data.title: TechnipFMC secures up to $1.25B in Exxon Guyana contracts
data.description:
TechnipFMC said post-market Thursday it was awarded two contracts by ExxonMobil to supply subsea systems for the Longtail development in Guyana's Stabroek Block.

TechnipFMC said the "large" contract, valued in the $500M-$1B range, covers project management, engineering, and manufacturing of a full subsea production system; the subsea architecture includes Subsea 2.0 trees, manifolds, and associated controls for the gas condensate development.

The separate "significant" contract, valued in the $75M-$250M range, covers the design and manufacture of flexible production risers for the Longtail development; the company said it will provide the same riser solution that was utilized on the Yellowtail and Payara phases of the Stabroek development.

TechnipFMC said Longtail is its eighth greenfield project working together with Exxon .

data.title: Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet to leave after nine years at company
data.description:
Ledger chief technology officer Charles Guillemet announced he will be leaving the company at the end of 2026, after nine years at the company.

In a post on LinkedIn on Thursday, Guillemet said he joined as chief security officer in December 2017, around three years after Ledger was founded. He launched Ledger Donjon, the company’s attack lab, a year later.

“We’ve been preparing this transition for many months, so Ledger’s teams, partners and roadmaps are ready. I’m bullish on Ledger’s future,” said Guillemet.

Guillemet has been a central figure in Ledger’s security operations, first as chief security officer and later as chief technology officer. He helped establish the Ledger Donjon attack lab, which tests hardware and software vulnerabilities. According to Guillemet, Ledger devices now secure roughly 20% of the world’s crypto assets.

“The threat landscape changed too. AI is making attacks cheaper, faster and easier to scale,” he added.

“The question we spent a decade answering for crypto (how do you protect what matters when any device can be compromised?) is now a question for every company, every AI agent and every government.”

Guillemet did not disclose details of his next venture but said he was “building something new” and would “dedicate my time to solving this security mess.”

Guillemet’s announcement comes weeks after Ledger disclosed that attackers had modified genuine hardware wallets with hidden components designed to capture users’ recovery phrases, and slipped the devices into authorized resellers.

The tampering cases were initially reported in Asia, with subsequent incidents identified in Europe and the United Arab Emirates.

data.description:
1847 ET - Japanese stocks may fall after Anthropic's listing failed to boost major U.S. stock indexes overnight. Nikkei futures are down 3.7% at 57600 on the SGX. The dollar is at 159.70 yen, compared with Y159.50 as of Thursday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on bond yields and crude oil prices, as well as any comments on the yen's recent weakness from Japanese government officials. The Nikkei Stock Average rose 0.7% to 59444.21 on Thursday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1841 ET - Australian unemployment has lifted materially since the Reserve Bank of Australia restarted its tightening campaign in February, says Joe Capurso, economist at CBA. By contrast, U.S. unemployment has trended lower this year. The divergence is reflected in market pricing for policy interest rates, he adds. The market is pricing another three 25bp increases in the U.S. by mid‑2027. By contrast, the market is pricing one and a half 25bp decreases in Australia by the end of 2027. The convergence in Australian and U.S. interest rates will continue to be a weight on the Aussie for months ahead, Capurso adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1840 ET - Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said that she supported holding rates steady in October as a matter of pace not direction, in a speech centered on the Fed's communications. Earlier this week, Fed governor Waller argued that the Fed should raise rates by 50 basis points next month, unless it can credibly signal that a quarter-point hike in December would be followed by another one in January. "A reaction function is also conditional: it tells you not just where policy is headed, but what would change it," according to her remarks. "I said I would want to move more quickly if inflation expectations drift up, if wage pressures build, or if underlying inflation moves higher."(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1840 ET - Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said that guidance about the rate path is less valuable in normal times because people can usually work out the path themselves if they understand the Fed's reaction function. "What matters in normal times is that understanding," according to text of remarks set to be delivered in New York on Thursday. When the Fed held interest rates steady in October, markets expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind where it needed to be, Paulson explained. "A shared understanding of the reaction function allowed policy to move deliberately and gave people time to adjust, without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop."(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1839 ET - Asian currencies consolidate against the dollar in early trade, but may be weighed by risk-off sentiment spurred by Wall Street's slide overnight. "Equity markets have been in focus and volatile," NAB's Gavin Friend says in commentary. With the broader U.S. market having slumped on Thursday, this equity weakness has led to risk-off trading, the senior markets strategist says. The U.S. dollar is little changed at 1,334.04 won and is flat at 1.2918 Singapore dollars, while the Australian dollar edges 0.1% lower to US$0.6649, LSEG data show. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

1833 ET - The Australian dollar remains near its year‑to‑date lows against the U.S. dollar and is weak against most of the cross rates too, says Joe Capurso, economist at CBA. The weak Australian jobs report for October on Thursday has led to a reassessment of the future path of the Reserve Bank of Australia's cash rate, he adds. It's a case of out with pricing a chance of a hike and in with 33 bps of cuts priced by this time next year. Unemployment rate divergence between the U.S. and Australia is causing interest rate convergence that is weighing on the pair, he says. The Australian dollar is trading around 66.48 U.S. cents. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1557 ET - Treasury yields edge lower as the Anthropic IPO fails to sustain risk appetite in Wall Street. The debut on Nasdaq values the AI company at nearly $1.5 trillion, but it doesn't keep investors from rotating away from risky assets. The resulting demand for Treasurys pressures down yields even as markets price in a cycle of Fed hikes. "The 10-year [Treasury] yield is still well over 5% and the small move down over the past week is indicative of a flight to safety," Cardiff's Dean Lyulkin said in an email. The 10-year yield declines 0.014 percentage point to 5.051% in a fourth consecutive fall. The two-year yield sheds 0.021 percentage point to 4.777%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1428 ET - Canada's small businesses may have a competitive advantage over box-box shopping this Black Friday: being local. Data from Constant Contact's holiday report suggests Canadian consumer demonstrate strong community loyalty. It finds 62.1% of consumer cite supporting local merchants as the top reason for shopping small. And almost 46% of Canadians do all or most of their holiday shopping in-person, with close to 51% saying they value unique local gifts and 32.5% looking for local shipping reliability. Constant Contact's U.S. survey shows that intentional support for small businesses has reached a multi-year high of 20.2%. (robb.stewart@wsj.com)

1404 ET - Precious metals futures remain under pressure as other commodities pick up from the previous day's rout. The extended decline in gold has more to do with profit-taking than failure as a safe haven, says Mauricio Di Bartolomeo, co-founder of Bitcoin-backed lender Ledn. "It's actually very rational for a gold investor to be very happy to take 50% to 100% in a matter of two to three years," he says. And with U.S. Treasurys paying around 5%, holders rotate into yield as gold probably can't guarantee that return from current levels for the next year, he adds. Front-month gold falls 1.5% in New York to $3,682.10 a troy ounce, its lowest since Sept. 19, 2025. Silver falls 1.5% to a 14-month low $44.318 a troy ounce. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1356 ET - Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate jumped 17 basis points to 7.28% this week, reversing four weeks of declines. Realtor.com Senior Economist Anthony Smith says hot inflation data and the persistence of the conflict in Iran will likely place upward pressure on bond yields and borrowing costs. The debate has now shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves. That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in rates through mid-October took its toll. The supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1228 ET - Home sales fell in New York State in October, while inventory and prices continued to rise, the New York State Association of Realtors says. October saw closed sales fall 6.1% from October 2025 to 10,042 this year. Pending sales also dropped, from 10,003 homes under contract last year to 8,949 last month. Prices rose 1.8%, to $435,000, compared to $427,100 in October 2025. Inventory also saw a rise, with inventory across the state increasing nearly 14% compared to a year ago, the Association added. Median sales prices have now increased year-over-year in 38 of the last 39 months, the group added. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1141 ET - The U.S. dollar's rise to a 20-month high is putting pressure on commodities broadly, including grains. "The dollar has softened slightly, allowing an overnight rally, however the dollar is again showing a little strength into the mid-session which is pulling values off their highs," says Brian Hoops of Midwest Market Solutions. Good early season growing conditions in South America and the stronger dollar have kept the grains in a solid downtrend, he says. "Until the technical trend changes or the dollar tops out, rallies will prove difficult to sustain." Corn is up 1.2% on CBOT, wheat is 1.9% higher and soybeans are off 0.3%.(anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

data.title: Japan Consumer Inflation Accelerates Amid Rate-Hike Views
data.description:
By Megumi Fujikawa

TOKYO--Japan's consumer inflation picked up slightly in October, reinforcing expectations for another interest-rate increase by the central bank.

Consumer prices excluding fresh food climbed 2.2% from a year earlier, following September's 2.1% gain, government data showed Friday. That compared with a 2.3% rise expected in a poll of economists by data provider Quick.

The acceleration comes as policymakers are becoming more worried about upside risks to prices stemming from higher energy costs, persistent yen weakness and rising semiconductor prices amid the artificial-intelligence boom.

The data likely fuels market views that the Bank of Japan will raise the policy rate again in December after lifting it to 1.25% in September. The central bank also declared last month that underlying inflation had reached 2% for the first time since the target was introduced in 2013.

BOJ Gov. Kazuo Ueda told a parliamentary committee on Thursday that the central bank remains prepared to continue raising rates to keep underlying inflation anchored around its 2% target.

Ueda also warned that core consumer inflation is likely to accelerate well above 2%, adding that currency fluctuations are increasingly feeding into domestic prices.

Write to Megumi Fujikawa at megumi.fujikawa@wsj.com

data.title: Fed's Paulson says understanding, not guidance, drives effective communication
data.description:
Key points:
  • Fed's Paulson says effective communications depend on understanding
  • Paulson says understanding Fed reaction function key
  • Paulson does not offer near-term rate guidance

By Michael S. Derby

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday central bank communications work better when officials and the public understand one another, rather than when Fed officials provide explicit comments about what they think lies ahead.

For the Fed, “understanding matters more than the specific ways we communicate,” Paulson said in the text of a speech to be delivered before a gathering held by the Money Marketeers of New York University.

“When we understand each other, we don’t need to say as much when new data arrive,” she said, adding, “You can anticipate how we'll respond, and we can act in ways that are steady and, for the most part, predictable.”

WARSH'S COMMUNICATION OVERHAUL

Paulson’s views on Fed communications come as the central bank has been overhauling how it explains its actions to the public. Under new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, the Fed has shortened its Federal Open Market Committee policy statement and has launched a special task force to weigh how the Fed should communicate its actions and views.

At the same time, Warsh has, in contrast to other recent Fed leaders, stepped almost entirely away from providing any guidance about the interest-rate outlook.

But even as Warsh has pulled back, many of his colleagues on the central bank have continued to provide regular updates on where they think interest-rate policy is heading and how the economy is faring.

Paulson did not offer any comments about the near-term outlook for interest-rate policy, as the central bank approaches its December 8-9 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, where it is widely expected to hike rates by a quarter percentage point, to between 4% and 4.25%.

Paulson said in her remarks that understanding how the Fed reacts to incoming data is particularly important.

“Communication works best when it builds a shared understanding of the reaction function, and that credibility is essential, because people act on messages they trust,” she said.

Paulson said an understanding of what the Fed is doing and why helped markets navigate the Fed’s decision to hold rates steady in late October after boosting them in September and signaling more hikes were in the works.

“In October, markets expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind where it needed to be,” she said. “A shared understanding of the reaction function allowed policy to move deliberately and gave people time to adjust, without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop.”
